enhanced.fullText:
The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA), codified at 42 U.S.C. §§ 9601-9675, commonly known as Superfund, establishes a comprehensive federal framework for addressing environmental contamination from hazardous substances. For higher education institutions, CERCLA creates significant liability exposure and compliance obligations related to current and historical contamination on campus properties.

CERCLA imposes strict, joint, and several liability on four categories of potentially responsible parties (PRPs) under 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a): current facility owners/operators, past owners/operators during disposal periods, hazardous substance generators, and transporters. Universities can face liability as current owners/operators of contaminated property, regardless of whether they caused the contamination. This liability extends to properties acquired through donation, purchase, or inheritance where previous activities may have resulted in environmental contamination.

The statute defines "hazardous substances" broadly under 42 U.S.C. § 9601(14), incorporating substances listed under the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, TSCA, and RCRA, plus additional CERCLA-designated substances found in 40 CFR Part 302. Universities conducting research, maintaining laboratories, or operating facilities using chemicals, solvents, or other regulated materials must ensure proper handling to prevent releases requiring CERCLA response.

Reporting obligations under CERCLA Section 103 (42 U.S.C. § 9603) require immediate notification to the National Response Center when hazardous substance releases equal or exceed reportable quantities specified in 40 CFR Part 302.4. Universities must report releases within 24 hours, with follow-up written reports as required under 40 CFR § 302.6.

The EPA implements CERCLA through the National Contingency Plan (40 CFR Part 300), which establishes procedures for site assessment, listing on the National Priorities List, and remedial action selection. Universities may face EPA enforcement actions under 42 U.S.C. § 9606 for imminent hazards or § 9607 cost recovery actions for cleanup expenses.

CERCLA's liability scheme provides limited defenses under 42 U.S.C. § 9607(b), including third-party defense, and affirmative defenses for innocent purchasers who conduct appropriate due diligence. The Small Business Liability Relief Act of 2002 added protections for bona fide prospective purchasers and contiguous property owners who meet specific criteria under 42 U.S.C. § 9601(35) and (40).

Enforcement penalties under CERCLA can be substantial, with cleanup costs often reaching millions of dollars. Universities face potential liability for natural resource damages under 42 U.S.C. § 9607(a)(4)(C) and may be subject to EPA administrative orders compelling cleanup actions. Non-compliance with CERCLA orders can result in penalties up to $37,500 per day under 42 U.S.C. § 9609 and 40 CFR Part 19.
enhanced.summary: CERCLA imposes strict liability on universities for hazardous substance contamination on campus properties, requiring immediate release reporting, environmental due diligence, and potential cleanup responsibilities regardless of fault.
enhanced.requirements:
## Liability Assessment and Due Diligence
- Conduct Phase I Environmental Site Assessments for all property acquisitions per ASTM E1527 standards
- Maintain documentation of appropriate inquiry into previous ownership and uses of campus properties
- Implement all appropriate inquiries defense requirements under 42 U.S.C. § 9601(35)(B)

## Release Reporting and Response
- Report hazardous substance releases ≥ reportable quantities to National Response Center within 24 hours per 42 U.S.C. § 9603
- Submit written follow-up reports as specified in 40 CFR § 302.6
- Implement immediate response measures to prevent further contamination migration

## Ongoing Compliance Management
- Establish hazardous substance inventory tracking for research and operations
- Train environmental staff on CERCLA notification requirements and response procedures
- Monitor EPA National Priorities List updates and regional enforcement actions
- Coordinate with state environmental agencies on voluntary cleanup programs where applicable

## Risk Management and Insurance
- Maintain environmental liability insurance coverage for potential CERCLA response costs
- Document continuing care obligations for any known contaminated areas on campus properties

Written follow-up reports required as specified by EPA regional administrators for significant releases.
